                                         REPLY COMMENTS OF
                                        ENCHANTED ROCK, LLC

         Pursuant to the Federal Energy Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”)’s October 27,

2025, Notice Inviting Comments in the captioned proceeding,1 Enchanted Rock, LLC

(“Enchanted Rock”) hereby respectfully submits these reply comments (“Reply Comments”) for

the Commission’s consideration in response to several initial comments related to the Secretary

of Energy’s proposed Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking.2 As previously indicated,3

Enchanted Rock generally supports the Secretary of Energy’s position regarding the need to

ensure “access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity” by facilitating the connection of

large loads “to the transmission system in a timely, orderly, and non-discriminatory manner.”4

Enchanted Rock hereby responds to the initial comments submitted by Vistra Corp. (“Vistra”),

the California Independent System Operator Corporation (“CAISO”), Constellation Energy

Generation, LLC (“Constellation”), Meta Platforms Inc. (“Meta”), and Google LLC (“Google”).

These Reply Comments reiterate the urgent need to facilitate load flexibility as a mechanism to

I.       REPLY COMMENTS

         a.        Need for Clear, Predictable Interconnection Rules

         The influx of large load facilities associated with the modern era of Artificial Intelligence

(“AI”) innovation is contributing to an unprecedented scaling of electricity demand requiring

solutions that consider long-term transmission planning, while acknowledging near-term

realities. Winning the AI race and bolstering the U.S. economy relies on the ability of federal

and state regulators to create stable and predictable rules that encourage infrastructure investment

and business confidence.

         Notably, Enchanted Rock agrees with Vistra that the regulation of transmission-level load

interconnections by the Commission “does not imply a diminution of state authority in the areas

that the [Federal Power Act (“FPA”)] reserves for state jurisdiction.”5 Vistra’s comments align

with Enchanted Rock’s initial comments seeking further clarification on the dividing line

between federal and state regulation of large load interconnection,6 and demonstrate the need for

the Commission to promulgate a final rule that is clear, predictable and legally durable.

         b.        Need for Alignment with NERC Reliability Standards

         In support of establishing rules to clarify the treatment of large load interconnections,

Enchanted Rock previously recommended that the Commission direct the North American

 Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) “to review and revise its standards to recognize the

flexibility created by large loads deploying on-site or co-located generation as a standard

operational and planning tool.”7 As Enchanted Rock indicated “[a]cknowledging load flexibility

during the transmission planning and interconnection processes allows transmission planners to

assume lower peak demand for the associated load facility, thereby reducing the immediate need

for transmission upgrades and expediting interconnection timelines.”8

         Enchanted Rock acknowledges CAISO’s comments that large loads connecting to the

transmission system pose significant impacts on system reliability,9 and supports efforts to

harmonize NERC’s reliability standards with the reforms being considered in this ANOPR

proceeding.10 Enchanted Rock believes that such harmonization will promote the timely, orderly

and predictable interconnection of large loads.

         c.       Need for Flexible Load Interconnection and Hybrid Resources

         Transmission system operators and planners urgently require a solution capable of

efficiently managing the high volume of large load interconnections and accommodating the

aggregate demand introduced by these facilities. As supported by the record in the captioned

proceeding to-date, operational flexibility provides a valuable means of supporting speed-to-

power.11 Indeed, hyperscale end-users, such as Google, have embraced the concept of gaining

speed through flexibility. For example, Google recommends that the Commission, in the near

term, prioritize “facilitating the integration of co-located generation, including electric storage

co-location and its practical application to facilitate speed-to-power, expedite study timelines,

protect ratepayer affordability, and reduce strain on transmission infrastructure. Indeed,

Enchanted Rock supports the Commission considering “near-term steps that can help set the

stage for longer-term solutions.”13

        Enchanted Rock’s initial comments in this proceeding also reflected these sentiments, in

particular, in discussing Enchanted Rock’s load co-located with dispatchable generation

(“LCDG”) model.14 Further, a joint study process would allow LCDG and hybrid facilities to be

studied based on their operational behavior and net load impacts, which Enchanted Rock

believes will result in less strain on the transmission system, unlock available grid headroom,

optimize existing transmission infrastructure and more accurately model the flexible capabilities

of the system. As such, Enchanted Rock encourages the Commission to adopt rules that will

facilitate joint study processes (even if only for a provisional period) and that evaluate co-located

and hybrid facilities based on their net impacts to the grid. Flexible models, such as LCDG, offer

a practical approach to meet accelerating energy “without driving up costs or abandoning

progress on efficiency, resilience and carbon reduction.”15 Growing demand “coupled with

        Further, Enchanted Rock acknowledges Constellation’s statement regarding the use of

interruptible service, that “if the customer chooses, interruptible service can serve as a bridge to

full service while transmission upgrades are completed.”17 Constellation appears essentially to

be describing a temporary, flexible service arrangement that, if allowed by the Commission,

would grant large loads the ability to operate prior to transmission expansions on an as-available

basis. Enchanted Rock notes that this concept aligns with aspects of Enchanted Rock’s proposed

LCDG model because it would facilitate “a temporary flexibility option that large loads can opt

into . . . therefore mitigate[ing] some . . . risks and allow[ing] for faster load interconnection.”18

        Other mechanisms of bridging, such as temporary power solutions, are applicable to co-

location configurations as well. Meta characterizes this as allowing “large loads to secure

electric power quickly, and, in some instances, streamline the build out of necessary transmission

infrastructure.”19 Data centers are able to connect to the grid faster “with options for incremental

capacity additions in the future.”20 Co-locating generation with load allows system planners to

II.     CONCLUSION

        Enchanted Rock appreciates the opportunity to submit these Reply Comments and

commends the Commission on initiating this proceeding. Enchanted Rock has drawn the ideas

and solutions discussed herein from various corners of the industry, with such ideas representing

key areas of common ground needed to move forward. Enchanted Rock urges the Commission

to prioritize the development of clear transmission interconnection rules and consider the value

of flexibility in accelerating large load interconnections, while protecting ratepayer affordability

and grid reliability.
